reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance, NAICS 52, at 41.0% of firms in the latest period, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The survey question asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the first time it was asked was September 2023. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than banking alone.

What banks are doing with the technology is tracked most directly by the Evident AI Index, which Evident Insights describes as an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across financial services. The index scores major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics, including talent, innovation, leadership and transparency, and this site's curated points call it the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. Evident also runs regional and adjacent editions, including an index for banks in Latin America, an index for banks in the Middle East and Africa, and an index for insurance, and it says its briefing has over 15,000 subscribers. Its own framing is that several of the world's biggest banks have quietly become AI-powered behemoths while tech companies took the early attention, and that banks are racing to incorporate the technology into almost everything they do.

On the governance side, banking is unusual because the rules predate the current wave. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance was issued in 2011, and this site's curated points note that credit and AML models already operate under it, making banking the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade. The letter appears in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. The curated points also describe a Treasury report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities and risks, as framing the US supervisory conversation. The excerpt harvested from the Treasury page in this dataset is about OFAC sanctions on a gold smuggling and money laundering network, so it does not itself supply detail on the AI report's contents.

The technical supply side shows up in one place here. This site's Financial Models section catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, with licence, downloads and release date, refreshed daily, drawn from the Hub's public API and sorted by all-time downloads. That is a catalogue of available models rather than evidence of bank deployment, and the material does not connect specific models to specific institutions.

The sources are largely silent on money and on returns. Nothing in this JSON quantifies vendor spending, investment totals or ROI in banking AI, and no source reports a measured return figure. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take three things from the material: the Census Bureau's 41.0% gives a sector-level baseline for finance and insurance, the Evident AI Index offers a comparative maturity benchmark across large banks, and the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 means model risk management expectations already apply, so governance is not a greenfield question in this sector. Beyond that, the material does not support claims about cost, payback or which specific use cases perform best.

https://evidentinsights.com/.brief: Evident Insights is an intelligence platform that benchmarks and tracks AI adoption across the financial services sector. It supplies data, research, and benchmarking to help financial services leaders make informed AI-related decisions, investments, and strategic choices. The platform publishes the Evident AI Index, which ranks banks and insurers on their AI deployment and highlights emerging trends. Since launching in January 2023, the index has sparked debate and received widespread press coverage, with Evident CEO Alexandra Mousavizadeh frequently commenting on global AI trends.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and states that the list is refreshed daily. It says the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page reports that it was last verified on 2026-10-03 and gives a citation format for the catalogue. It also notes that searches cover the full text of every published page on the site, which it says are all built from the same database.
